cards.q: When does a silicon diode conduct?
options: When its anode is more positive than its cathode by about 0.6 to 0.7 V
Whenever any voltage is across it
When its cathode is more positive than its anode
Only above 24 V
cards.why: Forward biased (anode positive) and past its forward voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon, it conducts. Reverse biased it blocks, up to its breakdown voltage.

cards.q: A bridge rectifier is fed with AC that peaks at {vp} V. Two diodes conduct at a time, each dropping 0.7 V. What is the peak of the DC output?
cards.why: In a bridge, the current goes through two diodes in series on each half-cycle: 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 V lost.

cards.q: Why is a diode fitted across a DC relay coil, pointing against the supply?
options: To give the coil's current a path when it is switched off, so the voltage spike cannot damage the transistor or output switching it
To stop the relay switching too fast
To rectify the supply
To light up when the relay is on
cards.why: A coil resists any sudden change of current. Switched off, it drives a large reverse spike; the flyback (freewheel) diode lets that current die away through the coil instead. It makes the relay drop out slightly slower.

cards.q: An NPN transistor switches a load between its collector and 0 V. What turns it on?
options: Current into the base, with the base about 0.7 V above the emitter
Voltage on the collector alone
Taking the base more negative than the emitter
Nothing: it is always on
cards.why: A small base current lets a much larger collector current flow. With no base current it is off.

cards.q: A transistor must carry a collector current of {ic} mA. Its current gain, hFE, is {h}. What base current, in mA, is the least that will do?
cards.why: Collector current is about hFE times base current, so the base needs at least $I_C \div h_{FE}$. In a switch you give it several times that, to be sure it is fully on.

cards.q: A {vin} V signal drives a transistor's base through a resistor. The base needs {ib} mA, and the base-emitter junction drops 0.7 V. What base resistor, in ohms?
cards.why: The resistor has the signal less the 0.7 V across it: $R = \frac{V_{in} - 0.7}{I_B}$, with the current in amps.

cards.q: For an ideal op-amp with negative feedback, which two rules let you work out a circuit?
options: No current flows into the inputs, and the output does whatever makes the two inputs' voltages equal
The output equals the sum of the inputs
The inputs draw as much current as the output gives
The output is always half the supply
cards.why: The inputs have a very high resistance, and the very high gain, held in check by feedback, drives the difference between the inputs to almost nothing.

cards.q: An inverting amplifier has a feedback resistor of {rf} kΩ and an input resistor of {ri} kΩ. The input is {vi} V. What is the output voltage?
cards.why: Gain = $-\frac{R_f}{R_{in}}$; the minus sign is the inversion.

cards.q: A non-inverting amplifier has a feedback resistor of {rf} kΩ and a resistor to 0 V of {rg} kΩ. The input is {vi} V. What is the output voltage?
cards.why: Gain = $1 + \frac{R_f}{R_g}$, and the output is not inverted.

cards.q: What does a low-pass filter do?
options: Passes low frequencies and cuts high ones, such as noise on a sensor signal
Passes high frequencies and cuts low ones
Lowers the voltage of a signal
Removes the DC part of a signal
cards.why: Low-pass: the low frequencies get through. That smooths a slowly changing measurement and takes off fast noise.

cards.q: An RC low-pass filter has R = {r} kΩ and C = {c} nF. What is its cut-off frequency, in Hz?
cards.why: $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}$, with R in ohms and C in farads (1 nF is $10^{-9}$ F).

cards.q: At the cut-off frequency of a simple RC low-pass filter, how big is the output compared with the input?
options: About 71%: 3 dB down
Half
Zero
The same
cards.why: At $f_c$ the output is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707$ of the input, which is −3 dB. The power is half, not the voltage.

cards.q: Why are the 24 V supplies in control panels switch-mode rather than linear?
options: They waste far less power as heat, so they are smaller and cooler for the same output
They give a cleaner output than any linear supply
They work without mains
They cannot be overloaded
cards.why: A switch-mode supply is typically around 90% efficient; a linear regulator burns the whole voltage difference as heat. Linear supplies are quieter electrically, which is why they survive in some measurement work.

cards.q: A linear regulator drops {vin} V to 5 V for a load of {i} mA. How much power does the regulator turn into heat, in watts?
cards.why: All the load current flows through the regulator with $V_{in} - 5$ across it: $P = (V_{in} - 5) \times I$.

cards.q: A switch-mode supply delivers {po} W to its loads at {eff}% efficiency. How much power does it take from the mains, in watts?
cards.why: Efficiency = out ÷ in, so in = out ÷ efficiency. The difference is the heat in the panel.

cards.q: When is the output of a two-input OR gate 1?
options: When either input, or both, is 1
Only when both inputs are 1
Only when the inputs differ
Only when both are 0
cards.why: OR: any input 1 gives 1. Only when the inputs differ is XOR; only both is AND.

cards.q: How many different values can a {n}-bit binary number hold?
cards.why: Each bit doubles the count: $2^n$. 8 bits hold 256 values, 0 to 255.

cards.q: A NAND gate has both its inputs at 1. What is its output?
options: It depends on the previous output
Half-way
cards.why: NAND is NOT AND: AND of 1 and 1 is 1, inverted to 0. Every other input combination gives 1.

cards.q: What does an ADC do?
options: Turns a voltage (or current) into a number the processor can use
Turns a number into a voltage
Adds two signals
Protects an input from overvoltage
cards.why: Analogue to digital. A DAC goes the other way, number to voltage, as in an analogue output card.

cards.q: A {n}-bit ADC measures 0 to 10 V. How big is its smallest step, in millivolts?
cards.why: The range is split into $2^n$ steps: $\frac{10}{2^n}$ V each.

cards.q: A signal contains nothing above 50 Hz. How fast must it be sampled, at the very least, to capture it without aliasing?
options: More than 100 samples a second
50 samples a second
25 samples a second
Exactly 50 Hz, in step with it
cards.why: Nyquist: sample at more than twice the highest frequency. Sampled any slower, the 50 Hz shows up as a false, lower frequency: an alias.

cards.q: In pulse-width modulation (PWM), what is varied to change the average power?
options: The fraction of each period the output is on: the duty cycle
The supply voltage
The height of the pulses
The direction of the current
cards.why: The output only ever switches fully on or fully off; how long it is on in each period sets the average.

cards.q: A {v} V supply is switched by PWM at {d}% duty. What is the average voltage?
cards.why: On for {d}% of the time at {v} V, off the rest: the average is {d}% of {v} V.

cards.q: PWM runs at {f} kHz with {d}% duty. How long is each pulse on, in microseconds?
cards.why: The period is $\frac{1}{f}$: at {f} kHz that is $\frac{1000}{{f}}$ µs. The pulse is {d}% of it.

cards.q: What is a PT100?
options: A platinum resistance thermometer: 100 Ω at 0 °C, rising with temperature
A thermocouple rated to 100 °C
A pressure transmitter with a 100 bar range
A 100-pulse encoder
cards.why: Pt for platinum, 100 for its resistance in ohms at 0 °C. It rises by about 0.385 Ω per degree.

cards.q: Using $R = 100(1 + 0.00385T)$, what is a PT100's resistance at {t} °C, in ohms?
cards.why: 0.00385 per degree is the standard average slope between 0 and 100 °C. For precise work over a wide range a transmitter uses the fuller Callendar–Van Dusen equation.

cards.q: An encoder gives {ppr} pulses per revolution on its A channel. The shaft turns at {rpm} rpm. How many pulses a second come from channel A?
cards.why: Revolutions a second = rpm ÷ 60; pulses a second = that times the pulses per revolution. Check it against the input's maximum frequency.

cards.q: A 4–20 mA signal cable's screen is often earthed at one end only. Why?
options: So no current flows along the screen between two earth points at different potentials: an earth loop
To save a terminal
Because screens only work at one end
So the signal can use the screen as its return
cards.why: Two earths a distance apart are rarely at exactly the same potential. Bond the screen at both ends and a current flows along it, coupling hum into the signal. For low-frequency analogue signals one end is common practice; the signal's return must never be the screen.

cards.q: Why are a variable-speed drive's motor cables kept apart from signal cables?
options: The drive's output switches very fast, and couples noise into cables run close beside it
The motor cable is hotter
It makes the cables easier to label
Signal cables slow the motor down
cards.why: The output is fast-switching PWM with steep voltage edges. They couple into anything alongside, so keep a gap and cross at right angles.

cards.q: How should the screen of a variable-speed drive's motor cable be bonded?
options: All the way round (360°) at both ends, at the drive and at the motor, through EMC glands or clamps
At the drive end only, with a pigtail
Not at all
To the neutral
cards.why: The screen carries the high-frequency currents back to the drive. A 360° bond at both ends gives them a short, low-impedance path; a long pigtail acts as an aerial. Follow the drive maker's EMC instructions.
